title: Identify, analyse and select business opportunities

lessons.title: Finding business opportunities
lessons.html:
Finding business opportunities

A business opportunity is a need that people have and are willing to pay for. Good ideas often come from problems you see every day. Look around your farm, village or town and ask: what do people struggle to get? What do they travel far to buy?

Where to look for ideas

  • Things people buy often: eggs, vegetables, bread, airtime, paraffin.
  • Services people need: fixing fences, ploughing small plots, transport to town, cutting grass.
  • Waste that can be used: kraal manure can be bagged and sold as compost to gardeners.
  • Seasons and events: people buy more meat in December and before Easter. Schools need uniforms in January.
  • Your own skills: if you can shear sheep, weld or drive a tractor, others may pay for that skill.

Listen to people

Ask people what they need. Listen at the taxi rank, the clinic queue and the shop. If many people say "I wish there was someone here who sold fresh tomatoes", that is a possible opportunity.

Example

Lerato noticed that the farm workers on three farms near her had to take a taxi to town to buy chicken. The trip cost R40 return. She saw an opportunity to raise broilers and sell them on the farms on pay day.

Write all your ideas in a notebook. Do not judge them yet. In the next lesson you will learn how to check each idea and choose the best one.

Remember that an idea is not yet a business. Many ideas sound good but nobody wants to pay for them, or they cost too much to run. That is why you must check every idea carefully before you spend money.

lessons.title: Checking and choosing the best idea
lessons.html:
Checking and choosing the best idea

Before you spend money, test each idea with simple questions. This is called analysing the opportunity.

  1. Who will buy? Are there enough customers close by?
  2. Will they pay enough? Can you sell at a price that covers your costs and leaves a profit?
  3. Who else sells it? If three people already sell eggs at the shop, can you do better, for example fresher or cheaper?
  4. What do you need to start? Money, tools, land, water, transport, skills.
  5. What can go wrong? Disease, theft, drought, customers not paying.

A simple cost and profit check

Lerato works out the cost of one broiler: chick R10, feed R55, other costs R10. Total R75. People on the farms will pay R95. Her profit is R20 a bird. If she sells 50 birds a month, she earns R1 000 profit a month.

Compare your ideas

IdeaCustomersStart costRisk
BroilersManyLowMedium (disease)
Bakkie transportManyHighMedium
Selling manureFewVery lowLow

Give each idea a score. Choose the one with enough customers, a cost you can afford and a risk you can manage.

Test small first

Start with a small batch, for example 20 chickens, and see if they sell. If they sell well, grow slowly. This protects your money.

Key points

  • An opportunity is a need people will pay for.
  • Look at daily problems, seasons, waste and your own skills for ideas.
  • Check customers, price, competition, start-up needs and risks.
  • Work out cost and profit per item before you start.
  • Choose the best idea and test it small first.
